catalog: Explore the fundamental AI algorithms used in simulations and game development. This course covers techniques like pathfinding, decision trees, behavior trees, finite state machines, and machine learning. Students will apply these algorithms to create more dynamic, responsive, and intelligent virtual environments. Ideal for those interested in game design, simulations, and AI programming.

goals.detail: AI algorithms such as pathfinding, decision trees, and behavior trees to create dynamic and responsive simulations.
the performance and effectiveness of different AI techniques in game and simulation environments.
intelligent behaviors for virtual environments by implementing AI-driven systems and solutions.
the use of machine learning algorithms in simulations, determining their suitability for specific scenarios.
a fully functional AI-drven simulation project that demonstrates the integration of multiple AI techniques.

assess.name: Micro-quiz
assess.description: Given spontaneously to assess understanding of something very recently discussed. Short (5 min or less). Small stakes.

assess.name: Presentation 1: The Pitch
assess.description: Students pitch their simulation world: what living system or phenomenon they want to model, why it interests them, and what their agent will do in it.

assess.name: Presentation 2: The Progress
assess.description: Students present the current state of their semester-long project.

assess.name: Presentation 3: The...Perfection?
assess.description: Students present the 'final' state of their semester-long project.

assess.name: Progress Reports
assess.description: At the end of each week, students will turn in a progress report, detailing what they have accomplished on their term project since the prior report. Must be *hand-written.*

assess.name: Quizzes
assess.description: A short in-class quiz each week on the prior week's reading and concepts.

instructions.Presentations:
Students will work on a term project throughout the semester and present that project over three talks.

Deliverable

By Sunday evening of the week of a presentation, students should submit their project in its most recent state as a single compressed (.zip) email attachment to the instructor.

Talk

Each talk will feature two primary, interwoven components:
  1. Demo. Prepared demonstration / explanation. The student prepares this ahead of time. Counts towards the grade.
  2. QnA. Dynamic question answering. Instructor initiated at various points during the demo. Student response assessed and considered toward grade assignment.

Students will be in front of the class for equivalent amounts of time during each presentation. What will vary between students is the amount of time spent on demo versus QnA. Demos that are informative and engaging will likely involve / necessitate less QnA, so it is in a student's best interest to make the demo portion(s) as informative and engaging as possible.

Durations

Presentation Duration
1: The Pitch 6 min
2: The Progress 8 min
3: The...Perfection? 10 min


Rubric

2 pts 1 pt 0 pts
Deliverable truency On time. Late.
Deliverable progress At or exceeding. Some work, but lagging. Well behind.
Demo representation Totally matches deliverable. Somewhat matches deliverable. Doesn't match deliverable.
Demo clarity Very clear. Somewhat clear. Not clear.
Demo engagement Very engaging Somewhat engaging. Not engaging.
QnA accuracy Answers fully correct. Partially but mostly correct. Frequently incorrect responses.
QnA clarity Answers completely clear. Mostly but not entirely clear. Answers pretty unclear.
QnA ownership Definitive ownership. Somewhat questionable ownership. Highly questionable ownership.


Notes

  1. Time limits are firm. Practice with a timer.
  2. Presentation order will be randomly determined by instructor ahead of time.
  3. Have a plan B for demo failures (recording, second machine, etc). Recovering well counts.
  4. Slides/notecards fine. Scripts and pre-loaded AI answers are not.
instructions.Progress reports:
On weeks we don't have a project presentation, you'll turn in a short, handwritten progress report. This is due at the start of class, on paper: notebook or printer paper is fine. Legibility and presentation is important and will be graded.

Head

  1. Your name
  2. Due date
  3. Topic(s) covered during the prior week.

Body

  1. What you got done on your project since your last report.
  2. How you worked the piror week's concept(s) into your project. Be specific: don't just say "I added loops," tell me what they're actually doing in your code and why you built it that way.
  3. Anything you're stuck on or still figuring out.

Notes

  1. Honesty is valued. If you barely touched the project one week, say that and explain what got in the way. An honest short report is better than a vague long one.
  2. Specific detail that shows meaningful understanding is essential to earn full points, not vague descriptions or padded length.
instructions.Semester project:
Students will work on a single large project throughout the semster. They will build it continuously from the first week of class through until the last week. Each time a new concept is introduced in class, students are expected to work that concept into their project in a way that is correct, meaningful, and observable.

What to build

Pick something you'll actually want to show people or use. You are going to be spending a lot of time on it, and the more excited you are by the idea, the more enjoyable your experience will be, and the better the project will be.

Assessment

There are two primary assessment modes:
  1. Progress reports. Most weeks, there will be a progress report due.
  2. Presentations. At three points throughout the semester, you will give a presentation on your work.

Progress reports

Every week (after the first week) that we don't have a presentation, you'll turn in a short written progress report covering what you did and how you integrated the prior week's concept(s) into your final project.

Presentations

Three times throughout the semester, you'll present your project to the class.
  1. Presentation 1. The Pitch. What you are building and why, plus whatever you have so far.
  2. Presentation 2. The Progress. Show significant progress with your project.
  3. Presentation 3. The...Perfection? Show the final state of the project (which won't be perfect, and that's okay).

What success looks like.

Overall, a highly successful project will be:
  1. Coherent. The components of the project fitt together in a way that makes sense. There aren't random for loops that do nothing that were added just so the project had for loops, for instance.
  2. Complete. Clearly uses everything we covered during the semseter.
  3. Smooth. Runs cleanly, without hiccups.
  4. Valuable. Does something genuinely useful or is really fun to interact with. No one needs a janky calculator app that they have to access through a terminal.
